long.title: A Year Without a Car
long.text:
When my old car finally broke down last January, the mechanic told me that repairing it would cost more than the car was worth. I was annoyed at first, because I had driven to work every day for ten years. But my sister suggested an experiment: why not try living without a car for a whole year? I laughed at the idea, but I agreed to try it for one month.
The first week was difficult. My office is eight kilometres from my flat, and I had to work out which buses to take. On the second day I got on the wrong one and arrived forty minutes late. My boss was not pleased. However, by the end of the week I had found a route that took only ten minutes longer than driving, and I could read on the bus instead of sitting in traffic.
After a month, I noticed some surprising changes. I was walking about six thousand more steps a day, and I slept better than I had for years. I was also saving money. Without paying for petrol, parking and insurance, I had almost two hundred dollars more each month. So I decided to continue the experiment.
Of course, there were problems. Shopping became more complicated, and I had to plan carefully before I went to the supermarket. Visiting my parents, who live in a village with only two buses a day, was the hardest part. A couple of times I had to borrow my sister's car, which she reminded me about often.
Now the year is over, and people keep asking me whether I will buy a new car. I'm still not sure. I miss the freedom of being able to go anywhere at any time, especially at weekends. But I don't miss the traffic or the cost. For now, I've bought a second-hand bicycle, and I've joined a car-sharing club for the occasional long journey. Perhaps that is the right balance for me.

long.title: Learning on the Job
long.text:
Most cafés hire staff who already know how to make coffee and serve customers. The Green Door café in Hue does the opposite. Every one of its waiters, cooks and baristas is a young person who has never had a job before. The café is part of a training programme for teenagers who left school early, and after six months there, most of them go on to find work in hotels and restaurants.
The idea came from Minh Chau, a former hotel manager. 'When I was interviewing people for jobs, I met so many young people who were clever and hard-working but had no experience,' she explains. 'Nobody wanted to give them a chance, so they couldn't get experience. I wanted to break that circle.'
Trainees spend their mornings in a classroom above the café, where they study English, food safety and customer service. In the afternoons they work downstairs with real customers. Mistakes happen, of course. 'On my first day I dropped a whole tray of drinks,' laughs Nam, who is seventeen. 'I wanted to run away. But the customers were really kind, and my trainer showed me how to carry the tray properly.'
Customers seem happy to be part of the project. Many of them are tourists who have read about the café online, but there are also local office workers who come in every day. A small notice on each table explains the programme and asks customers to be patient. 'The coffee is excellent and the service is friendly,' says one regular customer. 'If it's a bit slow sometimes, I don't mind at all.'
The café does not make much profit, and it depends on donations to pay for the classes. Minh Chau admits that money is a constant worry. But she has no plans to give up. Last year, forty-two trainees finished the programme, and thirty-eight of them are now in full-time jobs. 'That number,' she says, 'is the only profit I really care about.'

long.title: Why We Put Things Off
long.text:
For years I believed that I was simply lazy. I would sit down to write a report, check my emails 'just once', and look up two hours later having achieved nothing except a tidy inbox. So I was relieved, and slightly surprised, when a psychologist friend told me that procrastination has very little to do with laziness. 'Lazy people don't feel guilty about doing nothing,' she pointed out. 'Procrastinators feel terrible. That's the whole problem.'
According to researchers, procrastination is better understood as a problem of managing emotions than of managing time. When we face a task that makes us feel anxious, bored or uncertain, putting it off brings immediate relief. The bad feeling disappears, at least for a while, and our brains learn that avoiding the task is rewarding. The next time, the temptation to delay is even stronger. Unfortunately, the relief never lasts. The deadline gets closer, the anxiety returns, and it is usually worse than before.
Perfectionism makes matters worse. People who believe that every piece of work must be flawless often find it hardest to begin, because starting means risking a result that falls short of their own standards. As long as the task remains untouched, it can still, in theory, be perfect. Researchers have found that perfectionists are no more likely than anyone else to produce excellent work; they are simply more likely to produce it late, or not at all. Ironically, the fear of doing something badly is frequently what prevents people from doing it well.
This explains why the most popular advice often fails. Making detailed to-do lists or buying a new diary may feel productive, but it does nothing about the uncomfortable feeling at the heart of the problem. In fact, planning can itself become a form of delay: I once spent an entire afternoon designing a colour-coded timetable for a project I then failed to start.
So what does work? One technique that researchers recommend is surprisingly simple: make the first step so small that it is almost impossible to refuse. Instead of telling yourself to 'write the report', you decide to open the document and write one sentence. Once we have started, the task usually seems less threatening, and we often carry on far longer than we planned. Psychologists call this lowering the 'activation energy' of a task. A version of the same idea is to agree to work on something for just ten minutes, with full permission to stop when the time is up. Most people, it turns out, don't stop.
Another approach is to be kinder to ourselves. It sounds like the opposite of what a procrastinator needs, but a study of university students found that those who forgave themselves for putting off revision before one exam procrastinated less before the next. Self-criticism, it seems, simply adds to the negative emotions that caused the delay in the first place.
I have been trying both techniques for the past three months, with mixed results. The 'one sentence' rule has been genuinely useful, and this article is proof: I began it with a single line at seven o'clock this morning. Forgiving myself has been harder. Years of telling myself off are not easily undone, and I still catch myself calling myself names when I miss a deadline. But I no longer believe I am lazy, and that, oddly, has made it easier to get things done.

long.title: Starting Again: Four Career Changers
long.text:
A  Hoa, former bank manager, now a baker
'I spent fifteen years at the bank and, honestly, I was good at my job. The money was excellent, and I never imagined leaving. Then my mother became ill, and I took six months off to look after her. During that time I started baking bread every morning, mostly to keep myself calm. When it was time to go back to work, I just couldn't face it. My husband thought I'd lost my mind, and for the first year he was probably right: I was working twice as many hours for a third of the income. Things are more stable now. I've got four employees and a waiting list for my sourdough. I still miss the certainty of a monthly salary, though.'
B  David, former lawyer, now a secondary school teacher
'People assume I left law because I hated it, but that isn't true. I enjoyed the puzzles, the arguments, even the long hours. What I didn't enjoy was the feeling that my work only mattered to a few very rich clients. I'd always helped out at a youth club at weekends, and I realised that those few hours were the best part of my week. Retraining took a year, and it was humbling to be a student again at thirty-eight, surrounded by people half my age. Teaching is far more tiring than I expected. A day with thirty teenagers takes more energy than any court case did. But I've never once regretted the change.'
C  Linh, former engineer, now an organic farmer
'My decision was carefully planned. I didn't just wake up one morning and buy a farm. For three years I spent every holiday working on other people's farms, learning what the job actually involved, and I saved as much of my salary as I could. When I finally bought the land, I already had a business plan and a list of restaurants interested in my vegetables. My engineering background has turned out to be surprisingly useful. I designed my own irrigation system, which uses forty per cent less water than the one the previous owner had installed. The hardest thing has been the weather. You can plan everything, and then a single storm destroys a month's work.'
D  Marco, former chef, now a software developer
'Kitchens are exciting, but they're also hot, loud and exhausting, and after twenty years my back was telling me to stop. I'd always been curious about computers, so I signed up for an online coding course, just to see whether I had any ability. It turned out I did. The course was free, which was lucky, because I couldn't have afforded anything else at the time. Getting my first job was hard: many companies weren't interested in someone without a degree. In the end, a restaurant booking company hired me because I understood their customers better than anyone else in the office. These days I cook purely for pleasure, and I enjoy it far more than I used to.'

long.title: In Praise of Boredom
long.text:
There was a time, not so very long ago, when boredom was an unavoidable part of daily life. Waiting for a bus, sitting in a doctor's waiting room or enduring a long car journey, people had little choice but to let their minds drift. Today, that empty time has all but disappeared. The moment we have nothing to do, we reach for our phones, and the faint discomfort of having nothing to occupy us is relieved within seconds. Few of us would regard this as a loss. Boredom, after all, is unpleasant. Yet a growing number of psychologists are suggesting that in eliminating it, we may have deprived ourselves of something valuable.
The case for boredom rests largely on what it prompts us to do. In a frequently cited experiment, researchers asked one group of participants to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory, a task chosen precisely because it was so tedious. Afterwards, both this group and a control group were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had endured the dull task came up with significantly more ideas, and more original ones. The researchers concluded that boredom pushes the mind to search for stimulation, and that when the outside world provides none, it turns inwards and starts to generate its own.
It would be easy to overstate such findings. Laboratory studies of this kind tend to involve small numbers of participants, usually university students, and some attempts to repeat them have produced weaker results. Moreover, there is a difference between the mild, temporary boredom of a waiting room and the chronic boredom experienced by people trapped in monotonous jobs or isolated by illness, which has been linked to depression and risky behaviour. No one is seriously arguing that the latter should be encouraged.
What the researchers do argue is that the brief, everyday kind of boredom serves a purpose, functioning rather like a signal. Just as hunger tells us to eat, boredom tells us that what we are currently doing is not satisfying, and that we should look for something more meaningful. The difficulty with smartphones, according to this view, is not that they are harmful in themselves but that they silence the signal too quickly. We respond to the discomfort with the easiest available distraction, rather than asking what it might be telling us.
There is also the question of what the mind does when it is left to wander. Neuroscientists have identified a network of brain regions that becomes more active when we are not focused on any particular task. This so-called 'default mode network' appears to be involved in remembering the past, imagining the future and making sense of our own experiences. Some researchers believe that constant stimulation may limit the time this network has to do its work, although they admit that the evidence is still far from conclusive.
None of this means we should throw away our phones. The more modest suggestion is that we might occasionally resist the urge to fill every empty moment. Some schools have experimented with 'quiet time', in which pupils simply sit without books or screens for ten minutes, and teachers report that, after initial complaints, many children come to value it. For adults, the prescription may be as simple as leaving the phone in a pocket on the bus and seeing where our thoughts lead.
Whether this will make us more creative is uncertain. But it seems reasonable to suspect that a mind which is never allowed to be empty may also find it harder to be full.

long.title: How I Became a Scientist
long.text:
A  Dr Ana Ruiz, marine biologist
'I grew up a long way from the sea, so my fascination with it was entirely second-hand: books, documentaries, a poster of a humpback whale above my bed. When I finally saw the ocean at the age of fourteen, I was almost disappointed; it was grey and cold and nothing like the pictures. It took me years to understand that this was the real lesson. Science is mostly about the gap between what you expect and what you actually find. These days I spend months at sea collecting data that rarely confirms what I predicted, and I've come to enjoy that. My one regret is that I didn't study more maths at school. I spent my first year of university desperately catching up.'
B  Professor Kwame Mensah, astronomer
'My route was anything but direct. I trained as an accountant, because my family wanted me to have a secure profession, and I spent six years auditing companies' accounts. Astronomy was a hobby: I had a small telescope on the roof of our flat. What changed things was an online project that invited amateurs to classify galaxies in telescope images. I became rather obsessed, and one of the objects I flagged turned out to be genuinely unusual. The researchers who ran the project encouraged me to apply for a doctorate. I was thirty-one, and I'd be lying if I said I wasn't terrified. Oddly, my accounting background has proved useful. Much of astronomy is about spotting small errors in very large data sets.'
C  Dr Mai Tran, neuroscientist
'I can name the exact moment: a lecture in my second year of a medicine degree, when a professor showed us brain scans of a patient who could recognise objects but not faces. I remember thinking that if the brain could break in such a specific way, it must be organised in a way none of us understood. I switched from medicine to research the following year, which my parents found hard to accept. People imagine research is about brilliant ideas, but most of my week is spent writing applications for funding, and the competition is fierce. I'd tell anyone considering this career to be prepared for rejection. Most of my proposals are turned down, and you have to learn not to take it personally.'
D  Dr Jonas Berg, climate scientist
'I was not a promising student. I left school at sixteen and worked in a ski resort for several years, which, ironically, is how I became interested in climate. The older instructors kept telling me how much the snow had changed since they were young, and I wanted to know whether they were right or simply nostalgic. That question took me back into education through evening classes, and eventually to university. The answer, as it happens, was that they were right. I sometimes think my unconventional background helps when I talk to the public. I know what it's like to be sceptical of experts, and I try to show people the evidence rather than simply asking them to trust me.'

long.title: Lost and Found in Translation
long.text:
Every translator, sooner or later, is asked the same question: how much is lost in translation? It is usually posed sympathetically, as though the speaker imagines the translator as a kind of removal man, carrying furniture from one house to another and inevitably chipping a few chairs on the way. I have been translating novels for nearly twenty years, and I have come to think the question rests on a misunderstanding. It assumes that the original text contains a fixed quantity of meaning, which can only diminish as it is transferred. In my experience, the process is rather less tidy than that, and considerably more interesting.
Consider the simplest of examples. Vietnamese has no single word for 'you'; speakers choose from a range of terms that indicate age, status and degree of intimacy, and a shift from one to another can signal affection, respect or contempt. An English translator has no equivalent device. Something is indeed lost. But the translator who recognises this is forced to look elsewhere, to the rhythm of a sentence, a choice of verb, a carefully placed silence, in order to convey the shift in the relationship. Done well, the result is not a diminished copy but a different solution to the same problem, one which may draw a reader's attention to the relationship in ways the original, precisely because it was so effortless, did not.
None of this is to deny that some losses are real and irreparable. Wordplay is the most obvious casualty. A pun that depends on two meanings of a single word will rarely survive the journey, and the translator must choose between abandoning it, explaining it in a footnote, which is rather like explaining a joke, or inventing a new pun that does similar work. Each option involves a betrayal of some kind. Poetry presents still greater difficulties, since sound and sense are so closely bound together that to alter one is to alter the other. It is no accident that the most admired translations of poetry are often described as 'versions' rather than translations at all.
What troubles me more than these familiar problems, however, is the assumption, widespread among publishers and reviewers alike, that the best translation is an invisible one. A translation is praised when it 'reads as if it were written in English', which sounds like a compliment but conceals a demand: that the strangeness of the original be smoothed away. A novel set in rural Vietnam, in this view, should feel as comfortable to an English reader as one set in Yorkshire. Yet part of the value of reading in translation lies in encountering ways of thinking and speaking that are not one's own. A translation that removes every trace of the foreign may be fluent, but it is also, in an important sense, dishonest.
The opposite approach has its own dangers. Some translators, anxious to preserve the flavour of the original, produce English so awkward that the reader is constantly reminded of the effort involved, much as an overly elaborate frame distracts from the painting it surrounds. The challenge is to find a middle path: English that is natural enough to be read with pleasure, yet retains enough of the original's character to remind readers that they are, after all, somewhere else.
Cultural references pose a subtler problem. A passing mention of a festival, a dish or a popular song may carry, for its original readers, a whole world of associations that a foreign reader cannot be expected to share. The translator can add a few words of explanation, at the risk of slowing the narrative and patronising the reader, or leave the reference as it stands and trust the reader's curiosity. I have increasingly come to favour the second course. Readers, in my experience, are far more tolerant of not understanding everything than publishers tend to assume, and a little uncertainty can be part of the pleasure of being somewhere unfamiliar.
It is often forgotten, too, that translation can add as well as subtract. Readers of a translated novel sometimes notice qualities that the original audience took for granted, and a skilled translation can reveal patterns in a text that its own author never consciously intended. Several writers I have worked with have told me that reading their book in English showed them something new about it. One remarked, only half joking, that she now preferred my version to her own.
So when I am asked how much is lost in translation, I have learned to answer with another question: how much is found? The answer is rarely 'nothing', and occasionally it is 'more than you might think'.

long.title: Is Ambition Overrated?
long.text:
A  Helen Marsh, novelist
'I distrust the word, frankly. In my experience, the people who describe themselves as ambitious are usually describing a desire for status, which is not at all the same as a desire to do something well. texts: The shift to remote work has been hailed as a liberation. Freed from the daily commute, employees regain hours each week, and many report that they are able to concentrate more effectively away from the interruptions of an open-plan office. Employers, for their part, can recruit talent regardless of geography and reduce the considerable cost of office space. Yet the benefits are not evenly distributed: those with cramped accommodation or young children may find home anything but a haven of productivity.

What remote work gains in efficiency, it may lose in less tangible ways. Much of what makes organisations innovative arises from unplanned encounters: a conversation by the coffee machine, an overheard remark that sparks an idea. Junior staff, in particular, learn by observing experienced colleagues, something that video calls replicate poorly. There is also a risk that the boundary between work and private life dissolves altogether, leaving employees perpetually on call. A model that combines the flexibility of home working with regular time together may prove the most sustainable compromise.

Tóm đoạn 2: mất gặp gỡ ngẫu nhiên, người mới khó học, ranh giới mờ, mô hình kết hợp

m: Both texts examine the consequences of the move towards remote working, but they place the emphasis on rather different aspects of it.

The first text focuses on the practical advantages. Employees no longer waste time travelling and may find it easier to focus at home, while companies can hire people wherever they live and save on expensive premises. However, the writer rightly acknowledges that these benefits depend heavily on personal circumstances: parents of young children who live in a small flat are unlikely to find home a peaceful place to work.

The second text argues that something valuable is lost when colleagues no longer share a workplace. Spontaneous conversations, which often generate new ideas, become rare, and less experienced employees miss the chance to learn by watching others. The writer also warns that work may intrude into every part of private life, and proposes a hybrid arrangement as the solution.

In my view, the second writer raises the more serious concerns, since the advantages described in the first text are immediate and measurable, whereas the costs are gradual and easy to overlook. A young employee may appreciate the absence of a commute today without realising how much slower their professional development has become. Nevertheless, a hybrid model only succeeds if the days spent together are used for collaboration rather than for tasks that could be done alone. On balance, remote work is neither a liberation nor a threat in itself; its value depends on how carefully organisations design it.

texts: Mass tourism is frequently blamed for overcrowded city centres and damaged landscapes, but such criticism often overlooks its economic importance. In many regions, tourism provides employment where few alternatives exist, and the income it generates can fund the preservation of historic sites that would otherwise fall into disrepair. Visitors also bring cultural exchange, encouraging local communities to take pride in traditions that might otherwise be forgotten. The challenge is not to discourage travel but to manage it more intelligently.

The financial benefits of tourism are real but frequently overstated. A significant share of the profits ends up with international hotel chains and tour operators rather than local businesses, while residents face rising rents as homes are converted into holiday accommodation. Meanwhile, traditions risk being reduced to performances staged for visitors. Some destinations have begun to limit visitor numbers or introduce tourist taxes, arguing that only by restricting tourism can its long-term value be protected.

m: The two texts offer contrasting assessments of tourism, although both accept that it needs to be controlled in some way.

According to the first text, critics tend to ignore how much tourism contributes economically. It creates jobs in areas where there is little other work, and the money it brings in can pay for the upkeep of historic buildings. The writer adds that contact with visitors can strengthen local pride in cultural traditions, and concludes that tourism should be managed better rather than reduced.

The second text is considerably more sceptical. Its writer points out that much of the money spent by tourists goes to large foreign companies instead of local people, and that residents are often priced out of their neighbourhoods as properties become holiday lets. Far from preserving culture, tourism may turn it into a show. For this reason, the writer supports caps on visitor numbers and special taxes.

In my opinion, the second text presents the stronger argument, largely because it questions who actually benefits. The first writer's claims about employment are valid, but jobs in tourism are often seasonal and poorly paid, which limits their value to communities. That said, outright restrictions carry their own risks, particularly for regions with no other industry. I would argue that the most effective approach combines elements of both views: taxes reinvested in local housing and services, together with support for locally owned businesses, so that tourism serves residents rather than the other way round.

texts: Advances in machine translation have led some to question whether learning a foreign language is still worth the effort. Translation apps can now render everyday conversation with impressive accuracy, allowing travellers and businesses to communicate across language barriers instantly. For many practical purposes, the argument goes, the years spent mastering grammar and vocabulary could be devoted to more productive activities, while the technology itself will only continue to improve.

To regard a language merely as a code to be converted is to misunderstand what it offers. Learning another language gives access to ways of thinking, humour and social nuance that no translation fully captures, and it builds relationships of trust that are difficult to establish through a device. Research also suggests that the mental effort involved in language learning brings cognitive benefits, such as improved concentration, that extend well beyond communication itself.

m: Both texts consider whether translation technology has made language learning unnecessary, but they reach opposite conclusions.

The first text argues that machine translation is now accurate enough to allow people to communicate across languages without delay, whether they are tourists or companies. From this perspective, the considerable time needed to learn a language might be better spent on other things, especially as the technology keeps improving.

The second text rejects this view on the grounds that language is far more than a system for exchanging information. Knowing a language allows people to understand a culture's humour and subtleties and to build genuine personal connections, which a machine cannot achieve. The writer also refers to research showing that language learning improves mental abilities such as concentration.

I find the second text more convincing, although the first makes a fair point about practical communication. For a holiday, a translation app is undoubtedly convenient. However, the first writer assumes that communication consists only of exchanging facts, which is rarely true. Negotiations, friendships and even casual conversations depend on tone, timing and shared references that are easily lost when every sentence passes through a device. Moreover, relying entirely on technology leaves users helpless when it fails. In my view, translation tools are best seen as a support for learners rather than a replacement for learning; by making authentic material accessible to beginners, they may even make language study more rewarding. Learning a language, after all, is also a way of learning about the people who speak it.
